cosy-lesson.title: Are You Addicted to Drama? Why Some People Create Chaos in Their Lives

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: to introduce the topic and clarify key target vocabulary for the session.

cosy-slide.cosy-instruction: Review the key vocabulary for this session below:

cosy-blockquote.p: Adrenaline – a hormone released during stress, increasing heart rate and energy.

p.em: Example: High-conflict arguments trigger a sudden rush of physical adrenaline in our bodies.

cosy-blockquote.p: Addiction – the state of being enslaved to a habit or psychological dependency.

p.em: Example: Many psychologists describe drama-seeking behavior as a form of emotional addiction.
Example: Some people unconsciously create chaos in their relationships because peace feels boring to them.

cosy-blockquote.p: Validation – recognition or affirmation that a person's feelings are worthwhile.

p.em: Example: Seeking validation through constant complaints is a common but unhealthy social habit.

cosy-blockquote.p: Conflict – a serious disagreement, argument, or clash.

p.em: Example: Unresolved childhood wounds can make us repeat the same relationship conflict as adults.

cosy-blockquote.p: Subconscious – relating to the part of the mind we are not fully aware of.

p.em: Example: Our subconscious mind often seeks familiar patterns, even if those patterns are painful.

cosy-blockquote.p: Instability – the state of being unstable or lacking steady peace.

p.em: Example: Growing up in household instability can condition a child to expect constant crisis.

cosy-blockquote.p: Provoke – to stimulate or deliberately trigger a strong, angry reaction.

p.em: Example: It is unhelpful to provoke an argument just to test your partner's loyalty.

cosy-blockquote.p: Boredom – feeling weary and restless through lack of active interest.

p.em: Example: To escape quiet boredom, some individuals initiate gossip or dramatic rumors.

cosy-blockquote.p: Defense mechanism – an automatic mental reaction used to protect oneself from anxiety.

p.em: Example: Blaming others for your mistakes is a primitive defense mechanism that prevents growth.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: pair/group discussion on core session themes.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs or small breakout groups, discuss the following questions:

ol.li:
What is the cognitive mechanism that links a biological rush of adrenaline to drama-seeking habits?
※ Do you feel a physical urge to solve or fix problems immediately when a crisis occurs?

How does psychology explain how a constant search for excitement can turn into a literal addiction to crisis?
※ Have you ever had a friend who seemed completely unable to live without some kind of personal crisis?

What emotions are involved when a person unconsciously triggers relationship chaos to test their partner's love?
※ Do you feel anxious when your life becomes completely peaceful and quiet for a long time?

What operating cognitive biases explain why some individuals seek social validation by playing the victim?
※ How do you usually react when someone complains to you about the same issue repeatedly?

Why is interpersonal conflict often used as a defense mechanism to hide a person's deep-seated insecurities?
※ Have you ever started a minor argument just because you felt emotionally ignored or neglected?

What does psychology suggest we misunderstand about ourselves when our subconscious mind repeats painful family patterns?
※ Do you see any similarities between your current relationships and how your parents interacted?

How does growing up in childhood instability shape an adult's nervous system to expect constant stress?
※ Was your childhood home environment quiet and predictable, or was it highly spontaneous?

What cognitive triggers provoke a person to create dramatic situations when they are in a safe environment?
※ Have you ever felt a strong urge to disrupt a boring family gathering just to make it interesting?

How does acute boredom act as a catalyst for fabricating gossip or complex social rumors?
※ How do you handle boring administrative tasks without creating unnecessary distractions?

How can drama-seeking act as a protective defense mechanism to avoid confronting genuine emotional emptiness?
※ What is your primary strategy for coping with feelings of loneliness or lack of purpose?

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: collaborative task or visual analysis in pairs/groups.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs, work together on the following task:

cosy-blockquote.p: 🗣️ The Speculative Therapy Roleplay: Work with your partner to analyze a fictional "drama addict" case study. One of you plays the patient, and the other plays the wise therapist. Your Synthesizing Task: Explain the origin of this behavior and suggest healthier paths. You must explicitly structure your speech using: At least one Second Conditional (e.g. "If you learned to accept quiet moments, you would...") At least one Third Conditional (e.g. "If your parents had given you more stable attention, you wouldn't have...") At least one Mixed Conditional (e.g. "If you hadn't experienced childhood instability, your mind wouldn't crave chaos today...")

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: 1-on-1 guided visual description and task response with teacher.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: deeper debate and statement evaluation in pairs/groups.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs, debate and state whether you agree or disagree with these statements:

ol.li: If you could completely block your body's physical absorption of adrenaline during arguments, you would find it much easier to stay calm. (Second Conditional)
If psychologists had treated relationship drama as a literal neurological addiction decades ago, we would have developed healthier therapy methods by now. (Third Conditional)
If you hadn't experienced emotional chaos in your past relationships, you wouldn't feel so uncomfortable with quiet peace today. (Mixed Conditional)
If people didn't crave constant public validation on social media, online conversations would become significantly more peaceful. (Second Conditional)
If you had avoided that major conflict last year, your professional reputation would have been completely preserved. (Third Conditional)
If our subconscious mind didn't carry unresolved childhood wounds, we wouldn't repeat self-destructive relationship habits in our present lives. (Mixed Conditional)
If you were to live in absolute geographic and financial stability, you would quickly realize how much you miss spontaneous excitement. (Second Conditional)
If they hadn't tried to provoke their friends on purpose, they would not have lost their trust and support. (Third Conditional)
If you hadn't spent your teenage years in constant boredom, you wouldn't have developed a habit of fabricating gossip today. (Mixed Conditional)
If you were to recognize your drama-seeking as a primitive defense mechanism, you would stop blaming others for your personal stress. (Second Conditional)

ul.li: Incorrect: If I would be you, I would stop fighting. → Correct: If I were you, I would stop fighting. ((Underlined error: in the 'if' clause of a second conditional, use the past subjunctive 'were' instead of 'would be'))
Incorrect: She is addicted on drama. → Correct: She is addicted to drama. ((Underlined prepositional error. Correct collocation: 'addicted to'))
Incorrect: The chaos made me to feel anxious. → Correct: The chaos made me feel anxious. ((Underlined error: causative verb 'make' takes a bare infinitive without 'to'))
